extracted.intended_audience: writers, storytellers, public speakers and actors (literate 18th-century readership); anyone practicing narrative or oral performance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing and delivering stories, poems, and speeches—covering narrative surprise, plausibility, prose/poetic style, and the pronunciation/gesture rules for oral performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise is the life of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: “Surprize is so much the Life of Stories, that every one aims at it, who endeavours to please by telling them.” Surprise (a telling turn) is the element that most commands attention, produces sudden passion, or occasions laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-placed turns of surprise to engage and affect readers or listeners; it is more powerful than mere elegance of wording. Examples show how a sudden, well-managed surprise can elevate a tale's effect; anti-patterns include clumsy or gratuitous surprises that feel forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautifying graces do not replace substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Smooth Delivery, an elegant Choice of Words, and a sweet Arrangement, are all beautifying Graces, but not the particulars in this Point of Conversation which either long command the Attention, or strike with the Violence of a sudden Passion, or occasion the burst of Laughter which accompanies Humour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish (word choice, phrasing, arrangement) improves a piece but cannot substitute for the structural elements (surprise, conflict, humour) that truly seize the audience; prioritize dramatic/contentful moments over mere elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain probability; avoid outraging truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid over-leaping “the Line of Probability” or imposing a “kind of Nonsense against the Philosophy of Nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep events and details within believable bounds for your story's established world; inventiveness should not dissolve into implausible wonders or a 'heap of wonders' that strain credibility. The essay gives examples of conversational tall tales (miraculous effluviums of cheese, extreme antipathies) as anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manufacture improbabilities to gain admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a set of men who outrage truth, endeavouring only to make their hearers stare and so to 'glory at their expense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using false or improbable anecdotes to impress reduces the teller's esteem; audiences may respond with silence, scorn, mimicry, or indifference. Avoid fabrications or exaggerated claims intended merely to astonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience correction methods (social handling of implausible tales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common public responses to extravagant storytellers are a general silence (neglect/indifference) or 'over-shooting' them by replying with still more impossible stories to reveal the absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a writer/performer be aware of how audiences police credibility; a narrator who persists in improbability risks social correction. This is useful for shaping an author's rhetorical stance and anticipating audience reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation and action are essential to oratory and acting
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pronunciation and Action ... without which Part he affirms that the best Orator in the World can never succeed; and an indifferent one, who is Master of this, shall gain much greater Applause.” (after Cicero)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For spoken delivery (reading, recitation, stage), train both clear pronunciation and deliberate physical action—together they enliven and make language persuasive. The essay adapts Cicero's precepts for the British stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match voice tone to specific emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different emotions require distinct vocal qualities: anger = acute/raised/hurrying; sorrow = flexible/slow/interrupted/mournful; fear = low/hesitating/abject; courage = louder; pleasure = mild/tender/joyous; perplexity = grave/earnest/uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these associations when composing or performing dialogue and soliloquy; examples are given from Shakespeare and other dramatists to illustrate appropriate vocal modulation for each emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct action by the voice; gestures must enforce speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “As all these Varieties of Voice are to be directed by the Sense, so the Action is to be directed by the Voice ... The Arm ... is to be sometimes raised and extended; and the Hand ... sometimes to lead, and sometimes to follow the Words.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stage business and physical emphasis to support vocal delivery: raise or extend arms, lead with the hand, stamp the foot for command or anger. Action should underscore and be timed to speech rather than distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face and eyes are the primary expressive tools
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Face is the Epitome of the whole Man, and the Eyes are as it were the Epitome of the Face ... the best Judges among the Romans were not extremely pleased, even with Roscius himself in his Masque.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use facial expression and eye movement deliberately in performance and description; keep eyes mobile to convey feeling—an actor who fixes their eyes is an 'absent Actor.' In writing, highlight glance and countenance as compact conveyors of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of vocal tones and control pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Voices have a 'particular Medium and Compass' and 'the Sweetness of Speech consists in leading it through all the Variety of Tones naturally, and without touching any Extreme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train and plan for many tonal shades (gentle, rough, contracted, diffuse, continued, intermitted, broken, abrupt, etc.) and maintain a natural medium; use devices (practice, pitch reference) to avoid wandering into extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive facial shifts (beware buffoonery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not shift the form of the face on every occasion, 'lest it turn to Farce and Buffoonery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and judgment in expressive change; overacting of facial expression undermines seriousness and verisimilitude. Reserve larger shifts for moments that demand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action is a universal tongue; use gesture for broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “Action is a kind of Universal Tongue; all Men are subject to the same Passions, and consequently know the same Marks of them in others ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because gestures communicate across languages and literacy levels, incorporate clear, archetypal physical signs of emotion in performance and in vivid descriptive writing to reach a wider audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puns, affectations, and forced antitheses in elevated poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Spenser: 'no Puns, Affectations of Wit, forced Antitheses, or any of that low Tribe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In serious or high poetic diction, eschew cheap verbal tricks and showy conceits; prefer proper, fitting words and measured ornament. The essay links this to national poetic excellence (old words, exquisite numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and symbolism must suit their characters and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser's plan represents virtues by six legends/admirably drawn allegories 'suitable to their respective Characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using allegory or personification, ensure the symbolic elements coherently reflect the virtue or trait they represent; mismatched symbolism weakens moral or narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose apt imagery and epithets with justness and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'See what great Justness and Variety there is in these Epithets of the Trees ...' (praising Homeric epithets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select images and descriptive epithets that are precise and varied to enrich scene and character; avoid repetitive or tired metaphors—variety and aptness strengthen poetic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: When performing canonical works, preserve the original form
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint that a preacher who repeated Tillotson's sermon 'added and curtailed' and thereby spoiled it; a request: 'give them us as they find them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the integrity of well-known texts when reciting or adapting them—unwarranted additions or curtailments risk altering meaning and irritating audiences who know the originals.
